title: Origins and Road to War
sub: A new republic fights for survival

markers.label: Tallinn
markers.description: The provisional government had to build armed forces and state authority while enemies advanced.

markers.label: Narva frontier
markers.description: The Red Army attack at Narva opened the war for independence.

slides.title: Independence in the Vacuum of Empire
slides.cap: Estonian War of Independence visual reference.
slides.body: Estonia declared independence amid the collapse of the Russian Empire, German occupation, and the Russian Civil War. When German forces withdrew, the Red Army advanced to restore Bolshevik control. The new republic had to create an army, secure foreign support, and fight on multiple fronts before independence existed as more than a declaration.

stats.val: State-building and battlefield survival happen at the same time

title: Battle of Narva
sub: The Red Army opens the war

markers.label: Narva
markers.description: The Red Army attack at Narva marked the start of the Estonian War of Independence.

markers.label: Jaanilinn / Ivangorod
markers.description: The Narva River frontier became a contested gateway between Estonia and Soviet Russia.

slides.title: The Frontier Ignites
slides.body: The Battle of Narva began the war when Soviet forces attacked as German troops were leaving Estonia. The Estonian defense was fragile, but the battle clarified the stakes: either the new republic would build a fighting force quickly, or independence would collapse before it took institutional form. Narva became the eastern gateway around which much of the war's later fighting revolved.

stats.val: Soviet attack turns independence into war

title: Battle of Tartu
sub: Estonia recaptures a key southern city

markers.label: Tartu
markers.description: Recapturing Tartu helped secure southern Estonia and boosted confidence in the new army.

slides.title: Southern Estonia Turns
slides.cap: Estonian armored train troops associated with the liberation of Tartu.
slides.body: The Battle of Tartu was a key early Estonian success against Red Latvian Riflemen and Soviet-aligned forces. Recapturing the city helped restore government control in southern Estonia and proved that armored trains, volunteers, and newly organized units could reverse the Red Army's advance. It also gave the republic a psychological lift at a moment when survival was still uncertain.

stats.val: Southern Estonia begins returning to Estonian control

title: Battle of Utria
sub: A coastal landing threatens the Red flank

markers.label: Utria landing area
markers.description: Estonian and Finnish volunteer forces landed near Utria to threaten Soviet positions near Narva.

markers.label: Narva
markers.description: The landing supported operations aimed at retaking Narva.

slides.title: Amphibious Pressure Near Narva
slides.body: The Utria landing used coastal mobility to pressure Soviet forces near Narva. Estonian units and Finnish volunteers came ashore behind or beside the Red front, turning the coastline into an operational advantage. The battle matters because it shows Estonia's survival depended not only on holding lines, but on bold moves that disrupted a larger enemy's assumptions.

stats.val: Coastal maneuver supports the Narva counteroffensive

markers.label: Laagna
markers.description: Estonian marines and Finnish volunteers attacked Red Army positions near Laagna.

slides.title: Closing on Narva
slides.cap: Estonian War of Independence fighters near the Narva front.
slides.body: At Laagna, Estonian marines and Finnish volunteers fought Red Army positions as part of the wider effort to retake the Narva area. The engagement was local, but it belonged to a larger pattern: Estonia used small mobile formations, volunteers, armored trains, and coastal operations to regain initiative against Soviet forces.

markers.label: Paju Manor
markers.description: Heavy fighting around Paju Manor opened the route toward Valga.

markers.label: Valga
markers.description: Control of Valga mattered for southern communications and the Latvian front.

slides.title: A Fierce Southern Battle
slides.body: The Battle of Paju was one of the fiercest early battles of the war. Estonian forces and Finnish volunteers attacked Red Latvian Riflemen near Valga, suffering heavy losses, including the mortal wounding of commander Julius Kuperjanov. The victory helped secure the southern front, but its cost made it one of the war's most remembered engagements.

stats.val: Costly victory secures the Valga direction

title: Revolt of Saaremaa
sub: Internal revolt tests the new state

markers.label: Saaremaa
markers.description: The island revolt showed that the independence war also contained domestic social and political strain.

markers.label: Muhu
markers.description: The uprising spread across the western islands before being suppressed.

slides.title: War Behind the Lines
slides.cap: Estonian soldiers killed during the Saaremaa revolt.
slides.body: The Saaremaa revolt was an armed uprising against the Estonian government on the western islands. It reflected war weariness, social tension, resentment of mobilization, and the fragility of a new state trying to fight external enemies while imposing authority at home. Its suppression secured the rear but left a darker domestic chapter inside the independence struggle.

stats.val: Internal resistance exposes the strain of mobilization

title: Battle of Cēsis
sub: Estonian and Latvian forces defeat the Landeswehr

markers.label: Cēsis
markers.description: The battle checked Baltic German ambitions and strengthened Estonian-Latvian cooperation.

markers.label: Võnnu front
markers.description: The battle is remembered in Estonia as Võnnu, a major victory beyond Estonia's own border.

slides.title: A Baltic War Within the War
slides.body: The Battle of Cēsis was decisive in the conflict with Baltic German Landeswehr forces in Latvia. Estonian units fighting alongside Latvian allies stopped a German-led attempt to dominate the region's political future. The victory mattered beyond the battlefield because it protected Estonia's southern flank and supported Latvian independence at the same time.

stats.val: Checks Baltic German power in Latvia

markers.label: Krivasoo
markers.description: Late fighting around Krivasoo came as both sides approached exhaustion and negotiation.

markers.label: Narva front
markers.description: The eastern front remained central until the final ceasefire and Treaty of Tartu.

slides.title: The Last Hard Front
slides.body: Krivasoo was one of the late engagements near the Narva front before the ceasefire. By then Estonia had survived the most dangerous early months, but Soviet pressure still tested the eastern defense. The fighting showed why the eventual peace mattered: independence had to be won not only by declarations and victories, but by holding the front long enough to force recognition.

stats.val: Pressure continues until negotiations take hold

title: International and Human Dimensions
sub: Volunteers, British naval support, and a mobilized society

markers.label: Tallinn harbor
markers.description: British naval support helped secure sea access and deter Soviet naval pressure.

markers.label: Finnish volunteer route
markers.description: Finnish volunteers crossed the Gulf of Finland to support Estonia's army.

slides.title: A Small State With Outside Help
slides.body: Estonia's war was fought by Estonians, but outside support mattered. British naval power helped secure the coast, Finnish volunteers added manpower and morale, and events in Latvia and Russia shaped every front. Civilians faced mobilization, shortages, executions, occupation fears, and the uncertainty of whether a new state could survive the year.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: The Treaty of Tartu recognizes Estonian independence

markers.label: Tartu
markers.description: The Treaty of Tartu recognized Estonia's independence from Soviet Russia.

markers.label: Tallinn
markers.description: The new republic emerged with international recognition and a hard-won national army.

slides.title: Recognition Won by Force
slides.cap: Estonian soldiers after the independence struggle.
slides.body: The Treaty of Tartu ended the war and recognized Estonia's independence. That outcome was not inevitable in 1918: it required rapid mobilization, foreign help, victories against Soviet forces, success against the Landeswehr, and the ability to hold the Narva front until Moscow negotiated. The legacy became foundational for Estonian statehood, even after later Soviet occupation interrupted independence.
